Section 58

Footnotes

Footnotes

Introduction

fn1 Besides the ‘fructification theory’ (where interest is said to ‘derive’ from rent on land), there’s the surplus value (or profits) theory, productivity theory, ‘use theory’, ‘abstinence theory’ (spur to savings), ‘remuneration theories’, exploitation theory, reproductive theory and a number of Böhm-Bawerk’s ‘colourless theories’. To this list we should add Keynes’s notion, elaborated in his General Theory, that interest is required to discourage the hoarding of capital. Böhm-Bawerk rejected these explanations for interest, suggesting instead that interest arises because of man’s innate preference to enjoy present over future consumption. Needless to say, some economists deny the ‘time preference’ theory of interest.

fn2 Böhm-Bawerk was adamant on this point. Fisher, however, could conceive of situations when an individual’s time preference might turn negative. For instance, at times when incomes were declining rapidly, Fisher imagined that, if the stock of food was composed of spoiling figs, instead of hard tack, then the interest rate would be negative.

1: Babylonian Birth

fn1 Such folk, claims Mauss, were not motivated by ‘the cold reasoning of the merchant, the banker, and the capitalist … they repay with interest, but this is in order to humiliate the person initially making the gift or exchange, and not only to recompense him for loss caused to him by “deferred consumption”’ (Marcel Mauss, The Gift: The Form and Reason for Exchange in Archaic Societies, trans. W. D. Halls (London, 1990), pp. 96–7).

fn2 Marx calls Arnd’s theory the ‘primordial forest rate of interest’ (Marx, Capital, vol. III, trans. Samuel Moore and Edward Aveling (London, 1974), p. 363 fn).

fn3 Silver loans were made by weight, and barley loans by volume. One mina of barley was worth 60 shekels. Interest on silver was paid at the rate of one shekel per mina (1/60th per month or 20 per cent a year). There was a fixed exchange rate between barley and silver.

fn4 Assuming 20 per cent interest, paid annually and capitalized, Leemans calculates that the loan principal doubles with interest over 3 years and 283⅓ days (W. F. Leemans, The Old Babylonian Merchant: His Business and His Social Position (Leiden, 1950), p. 15).

fn5 There is no evidence that Einstein ever made this comment. The first known reference, according to the Quote Investigator website, is an advertisement for The Equity Savings & Loan Company published in the Cleveland Plain Dealer of Ohio in 1925: ‘The Eighth Wonder of the World – is compound interest. It does things to money. At the Equity it doubles your money every 14 years’ (https://quoteinvestigator.com/2019/09/09/interest/).

fn6 William Goetzmann comments that this is equivalent to 580 times the annual barley harvest of the United States (William Goetzmann, Money Changes Everything: How Finance Made Civilization Possible (Princeton, 2016), p. 35).

fn7 Clean slates limited the social disturbances that arose when borrowers fell into a state of debt bondage or had their lands foreclosed by creditors. Misarum acts only touched upon consumer (grain) loans, while commercial (silver) debts were unaffected. This suggests that the rulers were mostly concerned with the social consequences of excessive personal debt (Michael Hudson, ‘Reconstructing the origins of interest-bearing debt and the logic of clean slates’, in Debt and Economic Renewal in the Ancient Near East, eds. Michael Hudson and Marc van der Mieroop (Bethesda, Md, 2002), p. 7).

fn8 Morris Silver, Economic Structures of Antiquity (Westport, Conn., 1995), ch. 5 passim. Although it has been claimed that Ancient Greece lacked a true money market, a decree issued in the late fifth century BC by Plotheia, a district of Attica, calls for money to be lent out to borrowers offering the highest interest rate.

fn9 It is curious to note that the chief beneficiaries of Tiberius’ quantitative easing were patrician families. As we shall see, this was also the case when the Federal Reserve revived the practice in 2008.

2: Selling Time

fn1 ‘Debt was a deliberate device,’ writes Sir Moses Finley, ‘on the part of the creditor to obtain more dependent labour rather than a device for enrichment through interest’ (Finley, Economy and Society in Ancient Greece (London, 1981), p. 156).

fn2 Interest-free loans were available in Ancient Athens. Known as eranos loans, they were supplied by groups of lenders to be repaid when funds became available. Demosthenes claimed that the slave-prostitute Neara bought her freedom by raising eranos contributions from former clients.

fn3 Bonaventura’s comment contains the germ of Marx’s ‘labour theory of value’. In contradiction, Böhm-Bawerk pointed out that a bottle of wine, placed in the cellar, increases in value without any additional labour input.

fn4 Double-entry bookkeeping represents an extraordinary intellectual feat of quantification. Every asset and each exchange is given a monetary value and recorded in the same currency. The use of Arabic numerals enabled figures to be readily calculated. The German sociologist Werner Sombart, author of the six volume Modern Capitalism (first published in 1912), went so far as to claim that, by encouraging regular record-keeping, mathematical order and the reduction of events to numerical abstractions, double-entry contains the germ of the later Scientific Revolution.

fn5 Adam Smith, An Inquiry into The Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations [1776] (London, 1875), p. 44. Also, p. 285: ‘It may be laid down as a maxim, that wherever a great deal can be made by the use of money, a great deal will commonly be given for the use of it … Accordingly, therefore, as the usual market rate of interest varies in any country, we may be assured that the ordinary profits of stock must vary with it, must sink as it sinks, and rise as it rises.’

fn6 See Henri Eugene Sée, Modern Capitalism (New York, 1928), p. 125. Sée writes: ‘The present day meaning of capital was expressed, in the seventeenth century, by the word principal, or by the word interest. For example, such an expression as the following was used: “to take an interest of 5000 livres in a business.” Only in the course of the eighteenth century did the word capital really begin to take on its present meaning.’

fn7 Lionel Robbins, A History of Economic Thought (Princeton, 1998), p. 54. Ludwig von Mises made a similar point, writing in ‘Human Action: The Rate of Interest’ that anyone ‘who wants to “abolish” interest will have to induce people to value an apple available in a hundred years no less than a present apple’.

3: The Lowering of Interest

fn1 In The Nature and Necessity of Interest (London, 1903), Gustav Cassel calls Child’s comment an ‘evident absurdity’.

fn2 ‘As their critics pointed out, the directors [of the East India Company] maximized their return by refusing to issue more stock and trading on short-term, borrowed capital … they could profit, without investing more of their own capital, from the difference between the interest which they paid on bonds and the net profits of the trade. In 1683, however, a shortage of working capital created a temporary financial crisis. The stock fell in value and the company was forced to raise the rate on its bonds to 5 per cent in order to attract capital’ (extract from Sir Josiah Child’s entry in the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography).

fn3 Locke writes that ‘If lessening use [interest] to four per cent. should at all alter the quantity of money, and make it less, it would make money, as it has the nature of a commodity, dearer’ (Some Considerations of the Consequences of the Lowering of Interest and the Raising of the Value of Money [London, 1691], in On Money, vol. I (Oxford, 1991), p. 257).

fn4 Some of Child’s wilder ideas are still with us. ‘Low interest rates can cause a baby boom, Bank of England suggests’ ran the headline of an article in the Daily Telegraph on 23 December 2019.

4: The Chimera

fn1 The Genoese bank was created in 1407 by consolidating funded loans and distributing shares, luoghi, whose dividends varied with the tax yield. Law maintained an account with the Casa di San Giorgio, which he considered the ‘best governed [bank] in Italy’ (James Buchan, John Law (London, 2018), p. 81).

fn2 In Hamilton’s view, France’s ‘huge funded debt, the depreciated paper currency, and the acute commercial crisis were largely responsible for France’s acceptance of John Law’s scheme’. (See Earl J. Hamilton, ‘Prices and Wages at Paris under John Law’s System’, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 51(1), 1936, and ‘The Origin and Growth of the National Debt in Western Europe’, American Economic Review, 122, 1947.)

fn3 The issue at 500 livres in late 1718 was followed by another at 550 in the following June, rising to 1,000 in the next month, and 5,000 livres for the issues of September and October of 1719.

fn4 In the second half of 1719 only a 10 per cent down-payment was required on new issues. Subscribers were in effect buying options.

fn5 At this time a mason earned around 170 livres a year. The median US income is currently close to $59,000. Based on these relative incomes, Law paid close to $350 million in today’s currency for the Palais Mazarin. The building became the headquarters of the Company and the Royal Bank, and later housed France’s Bibliothèque Nationale.

fn6 When Law first approached the Regent with his scheme, the banker Samuel Bernard advised against it, saying there was ‘no foundation for the bank he proposes, in a country where everything depends on the King’s pleasure’ (Buchan, John Law, p. 111).

fn7 The definition of ‘realize’ is Washington Irving’s (from his 1825 essay, ‘The Great Mississippi Bubble’). An edict of December 1719 decreed that all public payments must be made in bank notes. The following February the import and wearing of precious metals, diamonds and pearls was banned and the Company was given the powers to search for hoarded coins. By the end of the month, only regulated goldsmiths were allowed to possess gold and silver.

fn8 Buchan writes that Law is invoking a ‘new species of property, where your capital is of use to the entire body of the nation’. Law’s autocratic desire to prevent money-hoarding foreshadows recent calls to abolish physical cash, to stop money being hoarded, at a time when central banks were attempting to impose negative interest rates (Buchan, John Law, p. 271).

fn9 ‘Law’s easy credit policy must have been largely responsible,’ wrote Hamilton, ‘for the failure of the market rate of interest to rise during the Bubble. In conformity with Wicksell’s theory, the disparity between the natural and the market rates of interest accentuated credit expansion and played an important role in the sharp upswing of prices’ (‘Prices and Wages at Paris under John Law’s System’, p. 63; see also François Velde, ‘John Law’s System’, American Economic Review, 97 (2), 2007).

fn10 In his ‘Essay on the Land Bank’ (written around 1704), Law criticized the rival land bank scheme of Hugh Chamberlen, who proposed supplying £10,000 of bank notes against land collateral, yielding an annual income of just £150 (i.e. a capitalization rate of 1.5 per cent), and attacked John Briscoe’s plan for a land bank which mooted an even lower lending rate.

fn11 That inflationary forces initially raise prices in some parts of the economy before becoming more widespread is known as the ‘Cantillon effect’.

5: John Bull Cannot Stand Two Per Cent

fn1 ‘Bad business takes time to grow – especially bad lending business, which is the most dangerous, because when discovered it saps credit, and destroys the spring of industry’ (Bagehot, Collected Works, vol. X, ed. Norman St John-Stevas (London, 1978), p. 37).

fn2 British government debt conversions at times of low interest were a coincident indicator of speculative booms and a leading indicator of financial crises, from the South Sea Company conversion of 1720 to the Goschen conversion of 1888.

fn3 ‘By freeing the funds of those who did not accept the new rate [on Consols] and by making current holders “restless” for a higher return on their funds, the conversion operations contributed somewhat to the floatation [sic] and Stock-Exchange boom,’ write Arthur Gayer, W. W. Rostow and Anna Jacobson Schwartz (The Growth and Fluctuation of the British Economy, 1790–1850: An Historical, Statistical, and Theoretical Study of Britain’s Economic Development, vol. I (Hassocks, 1975), p. 172).

fn4 The interest-rate cap on bills of exchange was abolished in 1833. In 1854, England’s usury laws were finally removed from the Statute Book.

fn5 Partner Henry Sykes Thornton, who was the eldest son of Henry Thornton, author of Paper Credit, took the whole affair on the chin, telling his sister: ‘what a great man breaking makes of me, I have had all these first-rate people trailing after me as if I had been Secretary of State. I always loved the character of a City Merchant and Banker, and it is delightful to see how they unite the powers of a man of business with the romantic effects of the heroes of fairy tales.’

fn6 The proposed railways included the Bristol & English Channels Direct Junction Railway, the Somerset & North Devon Junction Railway & Porlock Harbour & Docks, and the Bridgwater & Minehead Railway. None of these proposals got off the ground. In 1859, the West Somerset Mineral Railway opened to carry iron ore from the Brendon Hills to Watchet. It proved unprofitable. Watchet finally got its passenger line in 1862 with the opening of the West Somerset Railway. This line continues in operation to the current day.

fn7 This was standard practice for the time. After Overend’s failure, the Chancellor, Gladstone, advised by his ‘shadow chancellor’ Bagehot, allowed the Bank Act to be suspended on the condition that the bank rate was held at 10 per cent.

fn8 Argentina had been growing rapidly since 1870, following the ‘pacification of the Indians’ in the previous decade – between 1870 and 1890, its population doubled. In the 1880s, the country was under the stable rule of a strongman, General Roca. In the early 1880s, the currency was reformed – the new peso notes convertible into gold at par.

fn9 When it comes to lending to developing countries, the market’s capacity to recall past history varies in proportion to the domestic rate of interest: a low prevailing rate serves to fog the memory.

fn10 Paul Emden, Money Powers of Europe in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries (New York, 1937), p. 279: ‘[Argentine] railways were built to cope with a traffic far beyond the bounds of probability for many years to come.’ Over the course of the 1880s, the Argentine rail network expanded from 2,500 miles to nearly 10,000 miles. By 1893, some 13,900 miles had been completed.

fn11 H. G. Anderson, the Buenos Aires manager of the London and River Plate Bank, had long expected a crisis. In 1886 he informed his superiors in London that, as long as the Argentines continued to borrow, and to pay interest on old debts, the day of reckoning could be postponed. Anderson blamed the flow of foreign loans on low rates of interest in London (David Joslin, A Century of Banking in Latin America (London, 1963), pp. 121–5).

6: Un Petit Coup de Whisky

fn1 Treasury Secretary Shaw, who served under Teddy Roosevelt between 1902 and 1907, was said to conceive of only three evils: ‘high interest rates, a decline in the prices of stocks, and a contraction of credit, but these evils, in his opinion, were so serious that they were to be corrected at whatever cost.’ The author of this comment blamed successive Treasury secretaries for resisting with ‘all the vast resources of the government treasury the natural tendency of interest rates to follow the rising level of prices. They had, in fact, succeeded in keeping the money rate of interest below the rate which would have been “normal” or “natural” with a depreciating currency. They had kept alive a continuously excessive demand for credit, by making it available at less than the normal cost.’ (See A. Piatt Andrew, ‘The United States Treasury and the Money Market: The Partial Responsibility of Secretaries Gage and Shaw for the Crisis of 1907’, American Economic Association Quarterly, 9 (1), 1908: 228.)

fn2 Trust companies, such as the Knickerbocker Trust, were unregulated Wall Street firms (what would now be called ‘shadow banks’) that paid higher interest rates than savings banks and invested their deposits in illiquid and often speculative ventures.

fn3 Under the classical Gold Standard, inflows of foreign gold automatically added to a country’s gold supply. Under the Gold Exchange Standard, however, gold inflows could be ‘sterilized’ by a central bank issuing bonds. Thus, the specie-flow mechanism described by David Hume in the mid-eighteenth century no longer functioned properly and countries which received large gold inflows, as France and the United States did in the 1920s, were able to hoard large amounts of the world’s limited supply of gold.

fn4 The first reference to an ‘active monetary policy’ comes from The Economist in 1925, in reference to a 1 percentage point reduction in interest rates by the Dutch central bank.

fn5 Fisher was motivated by his belief that people confused real and nominal price changes. According to Fisher, ‘money illusion’ was an important cause of business fluctuations because wages didn’t fall in nominal terms at times when consumer prices were declining. This later became the ‘sticky prices’ theory of neo-Keynesian economists (see Perry Mehrling, The New Lombard Street: How the Fed Became the Dealer of Last Resort (Princeton, 2011), p. 57).

fn6 This point is explained by Bloomberg chief economist Tom Orlik: ‘As a rule of thumb, loan rates should be roughly in line with the pace of nominal GDP growth – a proxy for the expected return on investment. If they’re too much higher, no one will borrow, hitting growth and employment. Too much lower and demand for credit will be too great, fueling inflation and asset price bubbles.’ Orlik is writing about interest rates in China in the twenty-first century, but the point holds also for the United States in the 1920s (Thomas Orlik, China: The Bubble that Never Pops (New York, 2020), p. 73).

fn7 See Barry J. Eichengreen and Kris Mitchener, ‘The Great Depression as a Credit Boom Gone Wrong’, BIS Working Paper, September, 2003. The Federal Reserve also sterilized gold inflows from abroad, which further suppressed inflationary pressures. Perry Mehrling claims that Strong’s policy of keeping interest rates low and stable while sterilizing temporary inflows of gold ‘was the fuel that fired the stock market bubble … Inadvertently, Strong’s interest rate policy proved to be the original stock market put’ (Mehrling, The New Lombard Street, p. 41).

fn8 Both the cyclically adjusted price–earnings ratio and Tobin’s q measure of market value relative to replacement cost suggest that the US stock market was extremely expensive relative to its historic average valuation by the late 1920s.

fn9 In early 1929, Creditanstalt took over another Austrian bank, the Bodenkreditanstalt, that had financed long-term investments with short-term English and American credit. The latter bank foundered after American lenders withdrew. This acquisition turned out to be fatal for the Creditanstalt’s own future.

fn10 Felix Somary, The Raven of Zürich (London, 1986), pp. 146–7. Keynes and Fisher were not the only economists to hold sanguine views at the time. Somary mentions an evening at his home, held around the same time, where a number of distinguished German economists ‘all agreed that no crisis was in the offing because prices of goods had not risen at all; that sounded exactly like Keynes’s own views’ (Raven of Zürich, p. 153).

fn11 The nineteenth-century English economist W. S. Jevons, who developed a theory of marginal utility independent of the Austrian economist Carl Menger, likewise held that the level of interest determines the length of production processes.

fn12 ‘The rate of interest at which, in an expanding economy, the amount of new money entering circulation is just sufficient to keep the price level stable, is always lower than the rate which would keep the amount of available loan-capital equal to the amount simultaneously saved by the public: and thus, despite the stability of the price level, it makes possible a development leading away from the equilibrium position’ (Hayek, Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle, trans. N. Kaldor and H. M. Croome (London, 1933), p. 114).

fn13 By the date of the General Theory (1936), Keynes had lost faith in the notion of a natural rate of interest.

fn14 Ben Bernanke, ‘Asset Price “Bubbles” and Monetary Policy’, speech before the New York Chapter of the National Association for Business Economics, 15 October 2002. One question that Bernanke does not address is why the US economy was so much more vulnerable to high interest rates in the late 1920s than at the beginning of the decade. The answer is that intervening credit boom and various asset price bubbles had rendered its financial system unstable. History was to repeat itself during Bernanke’s time at the Fed in the early 2000s.

fn15 For further discussion see Chapter 10.

7: Goodhart’s Law

fn1 Although this book argues that price stability shouldn’t be the sole aim of monetary policy, this is not to say that inflation is desirable. The case against inflation is so well known it hardly needs recalling. Inflation damages economic growth by interfering with price signals and hindering long-term planning. It also distorts profits in myriad ways. Unanticipated inflation involves an unfair redistribution of income and wealth.

fn2 During his time at the Fed, Martin was bullied by President Lyndon B. Johnson to keep interest rates low. In December 1965, the Fed Chairman visited Johnson at his Texas ranch. The President took Martin for a fast drive in his jeep over a rough track in order to soften Martin up and induce him to cut interest rates. At an earlier meeting in the White House, President Johnson told Martin that raising rates would ‘amount to squeezing blood from the American working man in the interest of Wall Street’. In the end, Martin kept the punch bowl in place for too long and inflation took off under his watch (Paul Volcker and Christine Harper, Keeping at It: The Quest for Sound Money and Good Government (New York, 2018), p. 55).

fn3 Greta Kippner, Capitalizing on Crisis: The Political Origins of the Rise of Finance (London, 2011), p. 113. Kippner suggests that the Fed changed its policy after the October crash in order to use interest rates to support financial markets and to provide greater transparency and predictability. Henceforth, the Fed found that raising interest rates was politically more difficult.

fn4 The idea of creating a bubble to deal with a bubble had earlier been mooted by Paul Krugman in the New York Times in August 2002: ‘To fight this recession the Fed needs more than a snapback; it needs soaring household spending to offset moribund business investment. And to do that, as Paul McCulley of PIMCO put it, Alan Greenspan needs to create a housing bubble to replace the Nasdaq bubble …’ Krugman apparently found nothing wrong with this suggestion (Paul Krugman, ‘Dubya’s Double Dip?’, New York Times, 2 August 2002).

fn5 Ben Bernanke, ‘Monetary Policy and the Housing Bubble’, speech at the Annual Meeting of the American Economic Association, 3 January 2010. ‘Monetary policy following the 2001 recession appears to have been reasonably appropriate, at least in relation to a simple policy rule.’ This begs the question of whether the ‘simple policy rule’ was appropriate.

fn6 Bernanke, ‘Monetary Policy and the Housing Bubble’. Bernanke’s argument was based on a recently published paper by Fed researchers (Jane Dokko et al., ‘Monetary Policy and the Housing Bubble’, Federal Reserve Board, 22 December 2009). The paper’s authors claim that low rates in 2003–4 were justified on a precautionary basis due to the ‘significant risk’ of deflation (although they admit that subsequent revisions to inflation statistics showed deflation risk was exaggerated). Besides, they say, the Fed was only acting in a conventional fashion: the ‘setting of monetary policy appeared to follow the broad contours that would be expected given conventional macroeconomic views … outside forecasters, on balance, saw the policy stance adopted by the FOMC as consistent with the FOMC’s objectives’ (p. 13). They claim, rather disingenuously, that the US housing ‘boom’ started in 1998, long before the easy money policy commenced (as we’ve noted above, US house prices only exceeded 2 standard deviations above trend after 2002). The authors conclude that ‘all told, the evidence appears mixed at best on whether the policy stance of advanced economy central banks is among the significant factors contributing to the run-up in housing.’

fn7 In brief, the fall in Treasury yields after 2000 was due in large measure to the recirculation of international capital flows (Rueff’s ‘game of marbles’, in which the losses are returned by the winner), which took off after the Fed slashed rates at the turn of the century. This is discussed in more detail in Chapter 17.

fn8 In 2008, Schwartz wrote: ‘if you investigate individually the manias [of the past] … in every case, it was expansive monetary policy that generated the boom in an asset. The particular asset varied from one boom to another. But the basic underlying propagator was too-easy monetary policy and too-low interest rates.’ (Cited in Steven Horwitz and William Luther, ‘The Great Recession and Its Aftermath from a Monetary Equilibrium Theory Perspective’, Mercatus Center, October 2010, p. 5.)

fn9 For more on this theme, see Chapter 17.

fn10 In a 2003 speech, Bernanke had noted that inflation targeting was seen in the United States as something ‘foreign, impenetrable, and possibly slightly subversive’. Yet in his view, ‘low and stable inflation is a key element – perhaps I should say the key element – of successful monetary policy’ (‘A Perspective on Inflation Targeting’, p. 2).

fn11 Legend tells of a Soviet nail factory for which Moscow set quotas: when the quotas involved quantity, the factory churned out small useless nails, and when Moscow set a quota by weight, the managers produced railway spikes that weighed a pound each. The failure of central planning teaches that we should avoid the ‘tyranny of metrics’. In recent decades, however, the incautious use of performance indicators in universities and schools, healthcare, policing and business has produced a litany of errors. (See Jerry Muller, The Tyranny of Metrics (Princeton, 2018.))

fn12 See Chapter 15.

8: Secular Stagnation

fn1 George Terborgh, The Bogey of Economic Maturity (Chicago, 1950). Terborgh notes (p. 63) that the act of saving is not independent of investment (the purchase of a capital good). Thus, a decline in capital spending prompted by slowing population growth would automatically reduce saving. ‘Declining population growth tends to reduce both the volume of saving and the proportion of this reduced volume available for capital formation.’

fn2 The global savings glut hypothesis is examined in chapters 17 and 18.

9: The Raven of Basel

fn1 After 2008, the Federal Reserve signalled to the market its intended future interest-rate moves (forward guidance), acquired large amounts of securities (quantitative easing), and swapped its portfolio holdings from short- to long-date bonds (Operation Twist). All these actions were intended to lower long-term bond yields.

fn2 ‘One should not ask what the real side of the equation means for its financial counterpart, but what the financial side means for its real counterpart’ (Claudio Borio et al., ‘The International Monetary and Financial System: A Capital Account Historical Perspective’, BIS Working Paper, August 2014, p. 20).

fn3 ‘Overall, the results point in the same direction: no single real factor, or combination of such factors, can consistently explain the long-term evolution of real interest rates. This holds at both the domestic and global levels. It suggests that the observed correlation between the saving-investment factors and the real interest rate in the latest sample is largely coincidental, mostly driven by temporary but unrelated trends in the variables.’ (Borio et al., ‘Why So Low for So Long? A Long-Term View of Real Interest Rates’, BIS Working Paper, December 2017. See also Borio et al., ‘Monetary Policy in the Grip of a Pincer Movement’, BIS Working Paper, March 2018.)

fn4 Until the late 1990s, the trend level of real long-term rates was in line with its post-war average of around 3 per cent. fn5 ‘It is quite possible for inflation to remain stable while output is on an unsustainable path, owing to the build-up of financial imbalances and the distortions they mask in the real economy’ (Borio, ‘The Financial Cycle and Macroeconomics: What Have We Learnt?’, BIS Working Paper, December 2012, p. 9).

10: Unnatural Selection

fn1 Joseph Conard observes that interest rations capital on three dimensions: between the types of goods produced, between entrepreneurs and between methods of production (see Joseph Conard, An Introduction to the Theory of Interest (Berkeley, Calif., 1966), p. 95).

fn2 Karl Marx observed that ‘The rate of interest reaches its peak during crises, when money is borrowed at any cost to meet payments’ (Marx, Capital, vol. III, p. 361). Under the gold standard, the spike in interest rates during crises tended to be sharper as there was a scramble to convert a surplus of paper credit into a limited amount of bullion.

fn3 In his Treatise on Money (1931) Keynes wrote that the ‘most striking change in the investment factors of the post-war world compared with the pre-war world is to be found in the high level of the market-rate of interest’ (p. 337). At the time, Keynes believed that the market rate of interest in the late 1920s was above the natural rate. He later jettisoned the idea of a natural rate of interest.

fn4 This viewpoint is forcefully expressed by Boston University’s Perry Mehrling: ‘Credit is critical for the process of “creative destruction” that is the source of capitalism’s dynamism, because it provides the crucial mechanism that allows the new to bid resources away from the old. Instability is, from this point of view, inseparable from growth, and a central bank that intervenes to control instability runs the risk of killing off growth by stifling the new on the way up and coddling the old on the way down’ (Mehrling, The New Lombard Street (Princeton, 2011), p. 12).

fn5 Deutsche Bank concluded that the ECB’s actions had ‘curtailed the prospect of significant reforms in labour markets, legal systems, welfare systems, and tax systems across the continent’ (David Folkerts-Landau, ‘The Dark Side of QE: Backdoor Socialization, Expropriated Savers and Asset Bubbles’, Deutsche Bank Research, 1 November 2016, p. 1).

fn6 As George Soros told the New York Review of Books in January 2016, the Greek crisis taught the Europeans to muddle through, ‘this practice is popularly known as kicking the can down the road, although it would be more accurate to describe it as kicking a ball uphill so that it keeps rolling back down’ (George Soros and Gregor Peter Schmitz, ‘“The EU is on the Verge of Collapse” – An Interview’, New York Review of Books, 11 February 2016).

fn7 An IMF paper found that ‘increases in interest rates significantly affect job destruction, while reductions in interest rates fail to stimulate job creation’ (Pietro Garibaldi, ‘The Asymmetric Effects of Monetary Policy on Job Creation and Destruction’, IMF Working Paper, April 1997, p. 580).

fn8 See Andrew Smithers, Productivity and the Bonus Culture (Oxford, 2019). Smithers argues that equity-linked incentives caused senior executives of listed companies to become overly obsessed with their current share price and reluctant to invest for the longer term.

fn9 Claudio Borio, ‘A Blind Spot in Today’s Macroeconomics?’, BIS speech, 10 January 2018. The blind spot to which Borio alludes is the tendency of macroeconomics to ignore resource misallocations. A misallocation of resources between sectors is not possible in the canonical model which contains only a single company, the ‘representative firm’.

fn10 As William White wrote in 2012, ‘by mitigating the purging of malinvestments in successive cycles, monetary easing thus raised the likelihood of an eventual downturn that would be much more severe than a normal one’ (White, ‘Ultra Easy Monetary Policy and the Law of Unintended Consequences’, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, Working Paper 126, August 2012, p. 25).

12: A Big Fat Ugly Bubble

fn1 The Riksbank noted that very low interest rates in Sweden were ‘contributing towards [rising] housing prices and indebtedness among households’. Yet, interest payments by households had fallen to a record low of 3 per cent of GDP (Financial Stability Report 2015, Riksbank, 25 January 2016).

fn2 The gap between the earnings yield on stocks and the yield on risk-free government bonds is known as the ‘equity risk premium’. fn3 Grantham writes: ‘Pre-1997 real rates averaged 200 bps higher than now and leverage was 25 per cent lower. fn4 Monetary policy raised finance profits in various ways: lower interest rates pushed up asset prices, thereby increasing bank fees and asset managers’ incomes; losses on bad loans were curtailed; and, thanks to low borrowing costs and rising asset values, leveraged buyouts proved extremely profitable. Summers added that ‘low nominal and real interest rates undermine financial stability in various ways. They increase risk-taking as investors reach for yield, promote irresponsible lending as coupon obligations become very low and easy to meet, and make Ponzi financial structures more attractive as interest rates look low relative to expected growth rates.’ (See L. Summers, ‘Reflections on the New Secular Stagnation Hypothesis’, in Secular Stagnation, Facts, Causes and Cures, eds. C. Teulings and R. Baldwin (London, 2014), pp. 32–3.)

fn8 According to Stein, ‘low interest rates increase the demand by agents to engage in below-the-radar forms of risk-taking, this demand may prompt innovations that facilitate this sort of risk-taking’ (Jeremy Stein, ‘Overheating in Credit Markets: Origins, Measurement, and Policy Responses’, speech at the Federal Reserve Board, 7 February 2013).

fn9 In The City of London, vol. III (p. 391), David Kynaston describes a meeting of the Committee of London Clearing Bankers in November 1936, held at the Bank of England, where Governor Montagu Norman raised his eyebrows: ‘The Governor referred to the recent rise in Stock Exchange prices and the possibility of the existence of a position of over-speculation. While there was, in his opinion, no need at the moment for action he asked the bankers to watch the position carefully and to report to him in a month or two.’

fn10 In 2013, JP Morgan Chase announced it would hire some 13,000 extra compliance staff, at a cost of $4 billion. By the end of 2014, Citigroup was expected to employ more than 30,000 compliance officers (Sital Patel, ‘Citi Will Have Almost 30,000 Employees in Compliance by Year-End’, MarketWatch, 14 July 2014).

fn11 As Hyman Minsky observed, most financial innovation is intended to get around the regulations put in place after the last crisis. In this way, financial regulation resembles the Maginot Line, built by the French after the Great War to protect against another German invasion. During the Second World War, the German army simply bypassed this massive fortification by going through the supposedly impenetrable forests of the Ardennes.

16: Rusting Money

fn1 Banks use ‘risk-free’ US Treasuries as collateral for financial transactions known as repos. As the Fed’s QE reduced the float of Treasuries, these bonds weren’t available to be lent out or rehypothecated to foster private credit growth (see Gross, ‘Wounded Heart’, PIMCO Insights, 4 June 2013).

fn2 The fact that interest is necessary to get people to lend was observed by the early economists. As the merchant-economist Sir Dudley North wrote in the 1690s, ‘high Interest will bring Money out from Hoards, Plate, &c., into Trade, when low Interest will keep it back.’

fn3 On the deflationary impact of zombies see Viral V. Acharya et al., ‘Zombie Credit and (Dis-)Inflation: Evidence from Europe’, NBER Working Paper, May 2020. This paper claims that providing loss-making firms with credit resulted in excess capacity, which, in turn, ‘puts downward pressure on markups and product prices and thereby lowers inflation’.

fn4 Changes in household debt varied by nation. Between 2000 and 2008, US household debt climbed by 25 percentage points relative to GDP, and fell by 20 percentage points over the following decade. UK household debt followed a similar trajectory. In both countries, household deleveraging created a deflationary headwind. In several other advanced economies (including Sweden, Canada and Australia) consumer debt rose to record levels after 2008 (data from the BIS).

fn5 Discussed in the following chapter.

fn6 The taper tantrum is discussed in more detail in Chapter 17.

fn7 The Fed’s justification for QE3 was that ‘without sufficient policy accommodation, economic growth might not be strong enough to generate sustained improvement in labor market conditions’ (‘Federal Reserve Issues FOMC Statement’, Federal Reserve Board, 12 December 2012).

fn8 A meeting of the G-20 took place in Shanghai in February 2016, where it was agreed for the first time that countries would consult closely on foreign exchange rates. The markets dubbed this supposed informal agreement between central banks the Shanghai Accord, after the Plaza Accord of 1985. However, its existence was not officially confirmed. (See Rich Miller, ‘Shades of Plaza Accord Seen in Barrage of Stimulus after G-20’, Bloomberg, 17 March 2016.)

fn9 The ostensible justification for the Bank of England acquiring bonds issued by Apple and McDonald’s was that many issuers of sterling corporate bonds were not British companies, and it would have been invidious and market-distorting to discriminate against their paper.

fn10 In keeping with the political fashions of the day, Douglas’s acolytes were known as ‘greenshirts’ after the colour of their uniforms.

fn11 The Wall Street Journal cited the chief financial officer of the German industrial gas supplier Messer, who claimed that negative rates were a sign that ‘the economic situation isn’t improving.’ At the time, Messer was cutting investment and reducing debt. (Georgi Kantchev et al., ‘Are Negative Rates Backfiring? Here’s Some Early Evidence’, Wall Street Journal, 8 August 2016.)

fn12 In the early 1880s, new US banking regulations created such a fierce demand for Treasury bonds that the redemption yields on certain bonds turned negative. In the late 1930s, some US Treasury bills sold at negative yields because they were exempted from the personal property tax levied by some states. (See Sidney Homer and Richard Sylla, A History of Interest Rates, 3rd edn (Hoboken, NJ, 1996), pp. 285, 354.)

17: The Mother and Father of All Evil

fn1 Cross-border lending financed an overseas acquisition spree by Icelandic bankers, which included a faded English football club, a famous London toy store and a second-tier UK supermarket (coincidentally named Iceland). After accounting for the value of its foreign assets, Iceland’s net foreign debts amounted to twice its national income. The influx of foreign capital funded a current account deficit equivalent to a quarter of Icelandic GDP.

fn2 On 7 August 2007, the French bank BNP Paribas suspended redemptions on three funds that owned US mortgage securities. Cut off from the international capital markets, Northern Rock, a mid-sized British bank, closed its doors a few months later. Northern Rock’s was the first English bank run since Overend Gurney’s collapse of 1866. (See Viral Acharya and Sascha Steffen, ‘The Banking Crisis as a Giant Carry Trade Gone Wrong’, VoxEu, 23 May 2013.)

fn3 Jeremy Grantham, ‘Time to Wake Up: Days of Abundant Resources and Falling Prices are Over Forever’, GMO Quarterly Letter, April 2011. At the time of publication, the following industrial commodities were more than two standard deviations above their long-term price trend: lead (2.4 s.d.), platinum (2.4), oil (2.5), gold (2.6), nickel (2.7), palladium (3.4), silver (3.7), copper (3.9), coal (4.1) and iron ore (4.9).

fn4 The radical economist Henry George saw a connection between interest rates and wages, which arose from the competition between capital and labour: ‘interest,’ wrote George, ‘cannot be increased without increasing wages; nor wages lowered without depressing interest. For if wages fall, interest must also fall in proportion, else it becomes more profitable to turn labor into capital than to apply it directly; while, if interest falls, wages must likewise proportionately fall, or else the increment of capital would be checked.’ This is a keen insight. (Henry George, Progress and Poverty (New York, 1923), p. 199.)

fn5 In the five years after China joined the Word Trade Organization in 2001, manufacturing employment in Britain and the United States declined by a third. Displaced workers appear to have found less-well-paid, lower productivity jobs elsewhere. See Stewart Paterson, China, Trade and Power: Why the West’s Economic Engagement Has Failed (London, 2018).

fn6 By 2018, the US had a negative net international investment position of $10 trillion, a fivefold increase since before the financial crisis.

18: Financial Repression with Chinese Characteristics

fn1 Lien-sheng Yang, Money and Credit in China: A Short History (Cambridge, Mass., 1952), p. 97. The traditional reluctance of the Chinese state to pay interest is summed up in the comment of a late Qing official who stated that ‘as the loan is one from people to officials, it is inexpedient that it should bear interest.’

fn2 Richard von Glahn, Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000–1700 (London, 1996), p. 1. Glahn writes that ‘The state exercised greater direct control over money than over virtually any other facet of the economy, particularly since Chinese political economy deemed monetary policy the single most important tool of economic management at the ruler’s disposal.’

fn3 Between 1997 and 2002, bank deposits paid on average 3 per cent above the level of inflation. Over the following decade, the 1-year bank deposit rate, in real terms, averaged -0.3 per cent.

fn4 A 2010 BIS report states that ‘The household income share has also been dragged down by its shrinking net interest income. As a share of GDP, the net interest income halved in the past 15 years [to 2010], accounting for a quarter of the decline in the household income share’ (Guonan Ma and Wang Yi, ‘China’s High Saving Rate: Myth and Reality’, BIS Working Paper, June 2010, p. 18).

fn5 During this period there was a strong relationship between foreign capital inflows and the growth of deposits in the Chinese banking system.

fn6 By early September, the ‘national team’ of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) had spent an estimated 1.5 trillion yuan supporting the stock market, taking ownership of 9 per cent of the tradable shares (free float) on the mainland, according to Goldman Sachs. Other measures to support the market included a ban on short sales, forcing companies to engage in buybacks, strong-arming brokers into buying stocks, the relaxation of collateral rules on margin loans, and a halt to further IPOs. (See Kana Nishizawa, ‘China’s Stock-Rescue Tab Surges to $236 Billion, Goldman Says’, Bloomberg, 7 September 2015.)

fn7 The high occurrence of elevator accidents was partly due to the fact there were no condo associations in China and residents on lower floors often didn’t contribute towards elevator costs.

fn8 China’s steel consumption compounded at an annual rate of 15 per cent from 2000 to 2008 and maintained this growth level after the financial crisis. In 2009, steel consumption climbed by an astonishing 157 million tons. In 2017, the steel industry was operating at 70 per cent of capacity. (Dinny McMahon, China’s Great Wall of Debt (New York, 2018), p. 42; Nicholas Lardy, Sustaining China’s Economic Growth after the Global Financial Crisis (Washington, DC, 2012), p. 21; Thomas Orlik, China: The Bubble That Never Pops (New York, 2020), p. 14.)

fn9 Hong Kong Monetary Institute researchers Giovanni Ferri and Li-Gang Liu claim that the entire profitability of China’s SOEs (between 2001 and 2005) would have been wiped out had they been made to pay the same interest rates as private companies. Professor Christopher Balding of Peking University found that listed Chinese companies paid an average of 1.6 per cent on their loans in the first half of 2015, at a time when government debt yielded over 3 per cent. Balding estimates that a 5 per cent interest charge would have reduced reported profits by nearly 40 per cent (Giovanni Ferri and Li-Gang Liu, ‘Honor thy Creditors before thy Shareholders: Are the Profits of Chinese State-owned Enterprises Real?’, Asian Economic Papers, 9 (3), October 2010; Christopher Balding, ‘Guest post: Sizing up NPL risk in China’, Financial Times, 28 October 2015; for other SOE subsidies, see Usha Haley and George Haley, Subsidies to Chinese Industry (Oxford, 2013), p. 45).

fn10 Michael Pettis argues that the situation was actually worse than it appeared since Chinese investments were carried at cost in the GDP figures. As a result, even the worst investments boosted GDP while also lowering China’s reported ratio of debt to GDP (see Michael Pettis, ‘China’s Economy Needs Institutional Reform Rather Than Additional Capital Deepening’, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 24 July 2020).

fn11 Reuters reported that Chinese companies owed a total of $18 trillion, equivalent to 169 per cent of the country’s GDP. Only a quarter of mainland companies listed in Hong Kong had sufficient profits to cover interest costs. An official at one of these companies told Reuters that ‘There’s a lot of liquidity in the market and the interest rate is low … Borrowing from banks has not been a problem. Being an SOE also helps’ (Umesh Desai, ‘Road to Stagnation? China Inc Gets a Break from Lenders’, Reuters, 4 October 2016).

fn12 By early 2011 inflation was running above target and the People’s Bank of China had hiked the 1-year deposit rate three times. This coincided with a crackdown on shadow banks, which further undermined confidence among borrowers and lenders. Towards the end of the year, a court in Lishui sentenced three pyramid scheme operators to death.

fn13 In late 2015, an internet lender, Ezubo, was exposed as a genuine Ponzi scheme, whose reported 50 billion-yuan’s worth of investments turned out to be less substantial than the 12 million yuan pink diamond ring gifted by Ezubo’s chief executive to his mistress (Orlik, China, p. 47).

fn14 See Michael Pettis, ‘Why the Bezzle Matters to the Economy’, China Financial Markets, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 23 August 2021. Pettis argues that China’s bezzle includes the real estate market, where market values exceeding fundamental values created what Galbraith called a ‘net increase in psychic wealth’, and wasteful infrastructure projects that are entered at cost in the national income accounts. The total size of China’s bezzle, Pettis suggests, is roughly indicated by the country’s rising stock of unpayable debt.

fn15 In 1978, China’s Gini coefficient was 0.22. In 2001, Premier Zhu Rongji suggested that it would be intolerable for the Gini coefficient to exceed 0.4. When inequality passed this threshold in 2012, Beijing stopped publishing the data. (Evan Osnos, Age of Ambition: Chasing Fortune, Truth, and Faith in the New China (New York, 2014), p. 18.)

Conclusion

fn1 Even though US public debt climbed by over 40 per cent of GDP (2007–18), the government’s debt-service ratio was held at just over 2 per cent of GDP. In Japan, public debt doubled between 2000 and 2018, to reach nearly 250 per cent of GDP, but Japan’s debt-service ratio remained below 2 per cent of GDP. (See Charles Goodhart and Manoj Pradhan, The Great Demographic Reversal (Cham, Switzerland, 2020), p. 173.)

fn2 The Productive Finance Working Group was convened in November 2020 by the Bank of England, HM Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority ‘to develop practical solutions to the barriers to investing in long-term, less liquid assets’.

fn3 Strangely enough, this is what the Canadian economist Robert Mundell, the ‘father of the Euro’, originally envisaged. Mundell claimed that the European single currency ‘puts monetary policy out of the reach of politicians’, with the effect that ‘[b]othersome democracy is removed from the economic system’ (Michael Hudson, Killing the Host: How Financial Parasites and Debt Bondage Destroy the Global Economy (Petrolia, Ontario, 2015), p. 326).

fn4 For instance, in The Denationalisation of Money (London, 1990), p. 104, Hayek writes that ‘loanable funds made artificially cheap by creating more money for lending them, not only help those to whom they are lent, though at the expense of others, but for a while have a general stimulating effect on business activity. That at the same time such issues have the effect of destroying the steering mechanism of the market is not so easily seen. But supplies of such funds for additional purchases of goods produce a distortion of the structure of relative prices which draws resources into activities that cannot be lastingly maintained and thereby become the cause of an inevitable later reaction.’

fn5 Keynes’s widow, Lydia, was one of the many rentiers whose fortune was swept away by the rising tide of post-war inflation.

fn6 F. A. Hayek, ‘The Pretence of Knowledge’, lecture given at the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel award ceremony, 11 December 1974. As William White comments (in a personal email to the author): central bankers make a profound epistemological error by failing to treat the economy as a complex adaptive system. All their other errors are derivative.

Postscript

fn1 ‘Warren Buffett Wants to Make You Happier, Smarter and Richer’, Bloomberg, 2 May 2021. Three years earlier, Buffett had commented that ‘the most important item over time in valuation is obviously interest rates. If interest rates are destined to be at low levels … [i]t makes any stream of earnings from investments worth more money. The bogey is always what government bonds yield.’

fn2 Keynes had argued that people hoarded money because they expected a higher rate of interest in future. ‘Thus,’ wrote Robertson, ‘the rate of interest is what it is because it is expected to become other than it is; if it is not expected to become other than it is, there is nothing left to tell why it is – the organ which secretes it has been amputated, and yet somehow still exists – a grin without a cat.’
